set.descent_text: The route finishes on the summit plateau, after merging with the East Face line near the top. Descend by the Mountaineers Route to the north: from the summit, walk west across the plateau to where the route topped out, and note the spot, since the rim all looks alike from above. Steep, exposed third-class steps and ledges lead to the notch, then a long loose gully runs east to Iceberg Lake; some fourth-class downclimbing is possible near the top. Early in the season, or after storms, snow and ice can stay in the upper gully into summer, so carry an axe and crampons, wear a helmet against rockfall, and do not glissade the upper gully, where hidden ice can send you out of control. Parties have rappelled the icy upper section on slings left on the left side of the gully.
set.approach: From the Whitney Portal trailhead, follow the Whitney Trail a short way to the North Fork of Lone Pine Creek, where a climbers' trail leaves it and climbs a wooded slope into a willow-choked valley. Where the valley tightens, a third-class chute in the canyon wall leads onto the Ebersbacher Ledges, which skirt the worst of the brush and end at Lower Boy Scout Lake. Continue past Upper Boy Scout Lake over slabs, talus and moraine, then up a gully through the last band of cliffs to Iceberg Lake, the usual camp for the east side. The route begins from the scree below the second tower, up a corner that faces left, on the right-hand side of that tower and a few feet right of the East Face start. A Whitney Zone permit from Inyo National Forest is required: a day-use permit for a car-to-car push, or an overnight North Fork permit if you camp.

review.notes: MP east buttress: start at corner on right of second tower, descend Mountaineers Route; SMC: same camp/approach, rope-up right of East Face, joins East Face near top, descends Mountaineers; SP Mountaineers: approach details and usual east-face descent. REC: permits.

set.descent_text: Two ways down. One is to rappel from a slung block into the gully of the Mountaineers Route and follow that route down to Iceberg Lake. The other is to go on to the summit of the first tower and walk off, which is easy climbing but a little run out and links well with the East Face or East Buttress. The Mountaineers Route is loose, so wear a helmet and avoid knocking rock onto parties below.

A Whitney Zone permit from Inyo National Forest is required: a day-use permit for a car-to-car push, or an overnight North Fork permit if you camp.

review.notes: MP: descent options and start; Abegg: towers reached by scrambling from Iceberg Lake. SP Mountaineers: loose gully. Rappel count left out (single source).

review.notes: MP north face: route description and top-out at the summit, one party only. Descent per SP Mountaineers/SMC (usual descent).

set.descent_text: Finish on the flat summit area, then walk down the Whitney Trail, which is marked by cairns, past the saddle where the route began. The trail leads south to Trail Crest and then east down to Whitney Portal. Keep to the trail rather than the rim, because the wall below the summit area drops hundreds of feet and the rock near its edge is fractured.
set.approach: Take the Whitney Trail, from Whitney Portal past Trail Crest and north along the base of the summit mass, to the saddle that separates Whitney from Keeler Needle, which the trail passes close by. The climb starts in that saddle. A Whitney Zone permit from Inyo National Forest is required: a day-use permit for a car-to-car push, or the Whitney Trail overnight permit if you camp.

review.notes: MP SW edge: start at the notch next to the trail, finish on summit; trail descent per MP Happy Cowboy and Whitney Trail pages; REC: permits.

set.descent_text: The scramble ends on the flat summit area. Walk down the Whitney Trail, marked by cairns, back past the notch where the scramble started; the trail leads south to Trail Crest and then east down to Whitney Portal.
set.approach: Take the Whitney Trail, from Whitney Portal past Trail Crest and north along the base of the summit mass, to the saddle that separates Whitney from Keeler Needle, beside the trail. Leave the trail there and head northeast up to the summit area. A Whitney Zone permit from Inyo National Forest is required: a day-use permit for a car-to-car push, or the Whitney Trail overnight permit if you camp.

review.notes: MP SW ridge: start at the notch beside the trail, heads northeast to the summit area; trail descent per other MP pages; REC: permits.

set.descent_text: The traverse ends on the summit. Walk the John Muir Trail south to where it joins the Whitney Trail, continue to Trail Crest, then follow the Whitney Trail east, a long way down, to Whitney Portal. A permit for the Whitney Zone is needed year-round, so carry it for the descent as well.
set.approach: Follow the Whitney Trail from Whitney Portal up to Trail Crest, a long climb that many parties split with a night at Trail Camp, the highest dependable water. From the crest, walk north down the trail a short distance, stopping before the junction with the John Muir Trail, then scramble steeply east up loose scree and blocks until you reach the rim. Then swing north and stay on the crest of that rim. A Whitney Zone permit from Inyo National Forest is required: a day-use permit for a car-to-car push, or the Whitney Trail overnight permit if you camp.

review.notes: MP Happy Cowboy: start from Trail Crest and descent via JMT and Whitney Trail; MP Whitney Trail and REC: trail, Trail Camp and permits. Distances left out (not confirmed by two sources).

set.descent_text: Retrace the trail from the summit: follow it south to Trail Crest, then drop east past Trail Camp, Consultation Lake, Outpost Camp and Lone Pine Lake to Whitney Portal, over six thousand feet below the summit. The trail is usually clear of snow from midsummer to early autumn. In spring and early summer, snow and ice linger on the upper switchbacks, and an axe and crampons are needed for the descent as for the climb. A permit is required year-round for the Whitney Zone.

review.notes: MP Whitney Trail and REC: trail length, season, snow gear, camps and permits. Approach skipped: the trail is the route itself.

set.descent_text: Descend the Mountaineers Route. From the summit, walk west across the plateau to where the route topped out, and note the spot, since the rim all looks alike from above. Steep, exposed third-class steps and ledges lead to the notch, then a long loose gully runs east to Iceberg Lake; some fourth-class downclimbing is possible near the top. Early in the season, or after storms, snow and ice can stay in the upper gully into summer, so carry an axe and crampons, wear a helmet against rockfall, and do not glissade the upper gully, where hidden ice can send you out of control. Parties have rappelled the icy upper section on slings left on the left side of the gully. A longer, less technical alternative is to walk down the Whitney Trail from the summit and make a loop back to Whitney Portal.

review.notes: MP/SP/SMC: descent retraces the route, hazards (ice, loose rock, exposed third class, glissading); Abegg: rappel route on the left side of the gully when icy. Approach skipped: the existing row approach is not thin or is covered; only descent was set.
